newsitem.title: USA: NYS Assembly prepared to let rent rules expire.
newsitem.headline: NYS Assembly prepared to let rent rules expire.

text.p: The New York State Assembly Speaker, who has been fighting to preserve the present system of apartment rent rules, on Tuesday said he was prepared to let them expire in five days if no accord were reached.

Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, told reporters in Albany the budget was a sideshow to deflect attention from the real event, which was the battle over rent rules. The state again is repeating a pattern of late budgets as the latest pact for fiscal 1998 was due on April 1.

The Assembly Democrat argued the only difference between his position on rent rules and that of his opponents, Republican Gov George Pataki and the Senate Majority Leader, who both want vacancy decontrol, was how long it would take for that approach to eliminate the rules.

Asked if he were ready to let the rules expire on Sunday, Silver replied: "If need be, that's what vacancy decontrol does. It lets the laws die. The question is whether they die instantly, or they die a rather rapid death."
He spoke to reporters after meeting with Pataki and the Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy.

Under vacancy decontrol, apartments whose rents now are regulated would return to the free-market once tenants moved out. The Assembly, citing a 1971 to 1974 experiment with the policy that it says failed because landlords tried to force tenants out, has refused to go along with the policy, although Pataki would impose penalties on landlords who were found to have harrassed tenants. This has held the budget and a host of other issues.
Silver added that, if the rent rules did expire, he would continue his fight by showing the ill-effects of ending the present system.

Bruno, who has taken the toughest stand on the issue, told reporters that some of his members had asked him not to bring his version of a bill to the floor. Earlier, he and Silver differed over whether the Senate Majority Leader had enough votes to approve a one-house bill over potential objections by Republican senators from New York City, which has the state's vast majority of rent-regulated apartments, and from downstate counties that also have some of them.
The Republican Senate Majority Leader said that, while he would introduce a bill on Wednesday or Thursday, he had yet to decide whether to submit it to a vote in an effort to encourage a resolution.

"Again, I am doing my best to be flexible in terms of keeping our options open so that we can get a three-way agreement, because once I pass a bill and our members have had the vote, whatever the ramifications of that are, with amendments on the floor, which we will mow down, well, that's going to be a sort of a line in the sand, and I'd like to avoid that. But if we can't avoid it, then that's where we'll be."
